newsitem.title: UK: Dollar gyrations subside before EU, G7 summits.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gyrations subside before EU, G7 summits.

text.p: The dollar steadied after a week of gyrations, with traders expecting it to tread water before next week's European Union summit and a meeting of leaders from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations.

Expectations that EU countries will adopt a stability pact which promotes fiscal discipline after the launch of the European single currency has boosted the dollar as much as three pfennigs from the week's lows against the mark.
Dollar/yen, meantime, is looking to the G7 meeting for reassurance the U.S. is not about to start a war of words over a recent rebound in Japan's trade and current account surpluses.

Traders were loath to bet aggressively on dollar/yen before the G7 meeting. Waxing and waning trade concerns have seen the exchange rate set six-month lows Wednesday and then rebound 4 percent in the next trading session.

"Volatility is going to come down a bit pending the Denver G7 and the Amsterdam summit," said John Meisner, the manager of spot foreign exchange at Standard Chartered. "Dollar/yen, particularly, looks like it is going to settle back and consolidate after the massive moves we have seen."
The dollar was quoted at 1.7270/85 marks at 0750 GMT from 1.7260/65 late Thursday in Europe.
Dollar/yen was at 114.15/25 from 114.15/25 yesterday while dollar/Swiss franc was at 1.4415/25 from 1.4453/53 yesterday.

Hopes the G7 won't turn into a forum to criticise Japan's widening trade surpluses grew after U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said Thursday G7 leaders won't pay any special attention to U.S.-Japan trade flows, though the economic situation of both countries will be discussed.

Also, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said America will not use the dollar as an excessive instrument of trade policy. Still, he added that a sustained rise in Japan's trade surplus could hurt global growth and lead to a "protectionist backlash."

The focus on U.S.-Japan trade relations meant dollar/yen was little moved after a report Friday showed Japanese gross domestic product rose a larger-than-expected 1.6 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from the previous quarter and was up 6.6 percent from a year ago. Also, Japan's Economic Planning Agency said it expected consumption to pick up in the second quarter.

"The data was a bit stronger than people expected but they are scared of selling dollars after they got so badly hurt by the pullback yesterday and given that Rubin said the U.S. won't use the dollar as a trade tool," said Adam Cribben, the assistant chief trader at Credit Lyonnais.

Dollar/mark was also broadly steady. Talk of a possible delay to European economic and monetary union, which triggered mark gains earlier this week, subsided as EU officials said they expected an accord on a deficit stability pact which requires countries to maintain fiscal discipline after joining EMU.
France had triggered the talk of delay after it asked Monday for time to consider the pact.
German and French leaders meeting in Poitiers, France today are expected by traders to reiterate their commitment to launching EMU in 1999 and their intention of adopting the stability pact.
Traders are also looking to U.S. producer price data and the University of Michigan's sentiment index due today.

The unexpected drop of 0.4 percent in May U.S. retail sales in May raised doubts about whether the Federal Reserve will raise the target fed funds rate from 5.5 percent at its July policy meeting. Signs inflation is in check could add to such doubts and hamper dollar gains.

"I fundamentally like the dollar as the chances are rates will go up, even though the retail sales numbers yesterday made people pause for thought," said Meisner at Standard Chartered. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
